claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists in a high-temperature BCC phase.
Al is a relatively slow-diffusing element in this alloy.
Differential elemental diffusion during cooling produces local compositional segregation.
Slower Al diffusivity relative to the other elements produces local Al accumulation or depletion during cooling.
Local Al enrichment or depletion zones act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Cooling-induced compositional gradients lower the nucleation barrier for secondary-phase formation during subsequent thermal exposure.
Slow cooling will produce more localized Al segregation than rapid quenching.
After identical aging, slowly cooled samples will exhibit a higher incidence of secondary-phase formation than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and preserves a comparatively homogeneous BCC structure.
A rapidly quenched baseline is expected to exhibit minimal or no secondary-phase nucleation.
The proposed mechanism operates only when the cooling schedule and subsequent aging permit significant Al diffusion.
Extremely rapid quenching should suppress the proposed segregation mechanism.
Aging below the temperature required for appreciable Al mobility should prevent the proposed mechanism from producing significant secondary phases.
A lack of Al-segregation and secondary-phase differences between slow-cooled and rapidly quenched samples after identical aging would falsify differential Al diffusion as the driver.
